div.head: Rect 20, 20.1, 20.2
div.ab: Hæigwerde gebyreð þæt man his geswinces lean gecnawe on ðam en|dum ðe to etenlæse licgan forðam he mæig || wenan gyf he þæt ær forgymð þæt him man hwil|ces landsticces geann þæt sceal beon mid folc|rihte nyhst etenlæse forðam gyf he for slæwðe his hlafordes forgymð ne bið his ag|num wel geborgen gif hit bið ðus funden . gyf he ðonne eal wel gefriðað he healdan sceal ðonne bið he godes leanes ful wel wyrðe .

To the hedge-warden it is fitting that one knows that his labour’s reward [be] on the [field] ends which lie [closest] to the common pasture; because he can expect that if he first neglects that, that one [will hold] him [responsible] for whatsoever damage to the land. That [land which] is granted [to him] should be, by folk-custom, nearest to the common pasture, because if he should neglect his lord’s [land] out of laziness, [then] his own [land] will not be well-protected [either], if it is located thus. If, when all that he must tend is well-looked after, then he is fully well-worth a good reward.

[20] Hæigwerde gebyreð, þæt man his geswinces lean gecnawe on ðam endum, ðe to etenlæse licgan; forðam he mæig wenan, gyf he þæt ær forgymð, þæt him man . . . [20.1] … hwilces landsticces geann, þæt sceal beon mid folcrihte nyhst etenlæse; forðam gyf he for slæwðe his hlafordes forgymð, ne bið his agnum wel geborgen, gif hit bið ðus funden. [20.2] Gyf he ðonne eal wel gefriðað, he healdan sceal, ðonne bið he godes leanes ful wel wyrðe .
